projects.title: LangSmith Tool Gateway: a bouncer controlling your agents' tools
projects.what: A managed layer that every agent tool call goes through. Think Okta/1Password for agents: it decides which agent may use which tool, with which credentials, and keeps a trace of everything.
projects.how: 1) Register your MCP servers once (MCP is the standard for plugging tools like Gmail, Salesforce or GitHub into an AI), or enable built-in servers. 2) Build tool kits: a subset of tools behind a single URL; an agent connected to a kit only sees those tools. 3) Search mode: with hundreds of tools, the agent only loads the relevant ones so its context window does not overflow. 4) Identity: each call runs either as the user (their own access via Okta/Entra ID, with a sign-in link if they have not connected yet) or as the agent (shared service credentials for background agents). 5) Deny policies and human-in-the-loop approval for sensitive tools. 6) Every call is traced in LangSmith.
projects.who: The example is a large US retailer with 50+ MCP servers and 1,000+ tools: a store assistant acting with each associate's access, and an inventory agent running at 3 a.m. with its own credentials. Without a gateway, each team hand-rolls OAuth and nobody can audit. It is the missing piece when a personal agent becomes a team agent.
projects.try: Public Beta in the LangSmith Agent Platform (paid, price not stated in the article).

projects.title: LangSmith for Coding Agents: what each merged PR cost
projects.what: A dashboard that ties coding agent spend (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor...) to the pull requests they produce. In short, a cost per deliverable for AI-written code.
projects.how: LangSmith already traces every agent session (a trace is the step-by-step record of what the agent did and the tokens it used). The new 'outcomes' concept links each GitHub/GitLab PR to the threads that produced it (one session can open several PRs, one PR can take several sessions). The dashboard splits spend by PR state (open, closed, merged), isolates 'unattributed' spend (reviews, investigations that end without a PR), labels threads by work type (feature, bug fix, investigation, review) and shows the most expensive PRs and which skills are called.
projects.who: Coding is the largest enterprise AI spend category ($34B in 2026 per the article) and most leaders cannot say what it returns. Useful ROI metric to ask portfolio companies deploying coding agents about.

projects.title: Warp Factories: run coding agents like an engineered factory
projects.what: Warp CEO Zach Lloyd's vision: instead of managing a team of agents like coworkers (the Devin Bots approach, with a chief-of-staff agent delegating to designer and implementer agents), define a software factory in code: a cloud system of coding agents that is measured and improved continuously. From agent manager to production-line engineer.
projects.how: Per the tweet: the factory is declarative (you describe what you want, not every step) and versioned like code; all runs go through the cloud, producing standardized data; you measure with evals (tests that grade the agent's work, on your own data); you try other configurations (model, harness = the software wrapper around the model, skills); improvements ship as PRs. A closed loop, like continuous improvement in a factory.
projects.who: Platform teams that want to maximize throughput and quality of agent-written code while minimizing cost. Key argument: agents are not people, so for the first time we can directly measure how software gets made. Warp also released a hands-on course to build your own factory. Site not reachable during the run, details limited.
projects.try: Free course on Warp Learn; Warp Factories is a Warp product (price not read).
